chapter: Irish Channel youth, newspapers and McDonogh 35
title: Mardi Gras and the Irish Channel street gang
summary: He recalls watching parades, masking, and fighting in a neighborhood gang with Jonas Monroe, plus the mostly white bands he heard at Carnival.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: We were talking about holidays and things. When you were a kid, what did you do for Mardi Gras? How was Mardi Gras celebrated?

Well, when I was a kid, I would cross. My daddy would bring me to the parades when I was, you know, five, six, seven years of age. But as we moved on this side of the river when my mother and father separated, I started leaving 515 Third Street and walking down Jackson Avenue all the way to St. Charles Avenue and watched the parades. That's what we did. Now on Mardi Gras day, I would mask sometimes as a cowboy, sometimes as whatever. I felt like putting on and just hung out with my classmates, the friends who live in the neighborhood like Jonas Monroe and Timothy LeCore. These were my personal friends, you see, because we used to live together and go to school together, fight together and just terrorize the neighborhood together. Because I was a real bad kid for a while. Because I got, when I was on this side of the river mostly, I joined a gang, was a small gang. Well, you see, I tell you how it started. Before moving on this side of the river, we used to have to walk from the Jackson Avenue ferry all the way back to Hoffman High School. You know, at this time, I'm 13, 14 years of age. And a lot of whites used to meddle us. And we used to have problems with them. And sometimes we would catch one or two of us and beat us up until we decided to form a little alliance. And God bless the man soul today, I guess. And I'm asking the Lord forgiveness because I never forget one day some white guys were chasing us. And I ran across the street and I saw a big hunk of glass over there and it was the top off of a sugar jar. And this white boy was chasing me. And like you, throw a rock or something. I just slung it. Cut him green across the top. I almost took half his head off. And they'll forget that long as I lived. That's why I said I asked the Lord for forgiveness because I didn't know what I was doing. I just didn't want nobody to hurt me because I could always run fast, you know. But there in the 10th Ward and for the time that I lived over there for the three, three and a half years, I made a lot of friends. And we got together with our white friends. And let me tell you, something developed. After this encounter, the whites in the neighborhood, like a white boy by the name of Ellis, one by the name of Johnson, one white boy by the name of Washington. How a white boy get the name of Washington, I don't know. But I tell you, Ted, I know more black people with the name Washington than whites with the... You never thought about that. Because, see, a lot of blacks named their kids because George Washington was the father of the country. But whites looked like they shied away from naming... You could name me two or three whites. You know what the name of Washington. I know I can't. Well, I'm just having fun with it while we talk. But we formed an alliance. And the people, whites and blacks, who live on the other side of Jackson Avenue, when we catch them over there, come to visit the girls in our neighborhood, we used to fight them. And when we would go over there to visit their girls, they used to fight us. So could you imagine me, my black self, fighting with whites against other whites and blacks? That didn't last that too long. That was a lot of fun. But you fought with your hands then. It was Jonas Monroe, who used to beat me up all the time, who taught me how to fight because I was a runner. It took me a while to learn that when I started growing tall with these long arms and whatnot, that I could punch. Or then I started fighting and I became vice chairman of the neighborhood group or whatever. Well, it didn't have an official name. It just was a little gang that we used to get together and fight. It was a lot of fun in the world days up there in the Irish Channel. It was a lot of fun.
I had a question about Carnival because people, because you're looking at Carnival probably sometime in the 1930s, I guess.
Do you remember what music you heard on Carnival Day? Because it seems to have been changing.
